paras: The police beating of Edward E. Wilson took place on Monday morning, 14 September 1903, at the Harrison Street police station in Chicago, where officers seized, struck and locked up Wilson, a lawyer, after he disobeyed an order to take a seat. Wilson, described as a "Neger" by the Polish-language Dziennik Chicagoski, sued the officers for $10,000.

Wilson had come to the station's court to handle a client's case. According to the Chicago Broad Ax, Bailiff Griffin ordered him to sit among the crowd, and when he refused, four or five officers dealt him "several violent blows" and smashed his hat. Inspector P. J. Lavin then ordered him thrown downstairs and locked up.

Dziennik Chicagoski gave the court's version: Judge Caverly ordered the unruly audience to sit, Wilson alone ignored him, and when sent to the lockup he resisted the bailiff until policemen joined in. He ended up in a cell with welts on his back and a bruised nose.

Although Attorney John G. Jones signed his bond, Wilson was held another half hour. By 19 September he had sued Inspector Lavin, Sergeants Cannon and McCann and other officers in the circuit court for $10,000. No report of the suit's outcome was found.

Dziennik Chicagoski, the only white paper found to report it, headlined the item "Adwokat wlasnej sprawy" (Lawyer in his own case), called Wilson "uparty Neger" (a stubborn Negro) and joked that not even Hercules could resist the whole squad. It allowed, though, that the police had obeyed the court "zbyt energicznie" (too energetically).

The Broad Ax ran the story four days later in its front-page "Club Notes" and took Wilson's side, calling the station "a den" and the officers "brutal and cowardly" men who acted "as though they had been drinking Irish whisky." Neither paper presented the beating as racially motivated.
The Broad Ax attributed the orders to Bailiff Griffin and Inspector Lavin, Dziennik Chicagoski to Judge Caverly, and only the Polish daily said Wilson resisted.

reader.title: Police beating of Edward E. Wilson
bases: Both reports describe police officers at the Harrison Street station seizing, striking and locking up a lawyer who did not obey an order to sit, with no crowd or mob involved (A1, A2).

A Polish-language white daily (A1) and the Black Chicago Broad Ax (A2) independently report that lawyer Edward E. Wilson refused an order to sit at the Harrison Street station, was seized by police, injured and locked up, and meant to sue the officers, though they differ on who gave the orders and on his resistance.

accounts.label: Black weekly (Broad Ax)
accounts.gist: Wilson refused Bailiff Griffin's order to sit among the crowd and was seized by four or five officers who beat him and smashed his hat; Inspector Lavin had him thrown downstairs and locked up, and he was held even after bond was signed.

accounts.label: Polish-language daily (court's side)
accounts.gist: The courtroom was unruly, Judge Caverly ordered all to sit, and Wilson alone repeatedly ignored him; ordered to the lockup, he resisted the bailiff, police joined in, and he was locked up with welts and a bruised nose.

framing.detail: A 'Club Notes' item calling the station 'a den', the officers 'brutal and cowardly' and seemingly drunk on 'Irish whisky', and Lavin 'entirely unfitted' for his post, ending with Wilson's vow to 'fight them to the bitter end'.

Headlined 'Adwokat wlasnej sprawy' (Lawyer in his own case), it calls Wilson 'uparty Neger' and jokes that not even Hercules could resist the whole squad, yet says the police obeyed the court 'zbyt energicznie' (too energetically).

versions.value: Bailiff Griffin ordered Wilson to sit; Inspector P. J. Lavin ordered him thrown downstairs and locked up
Judge Caverly ordered all present to sit and then ordered the bailiff to take Wilson to the lockup

conflicts.note: Neither paper's account excludes the other entirely; the Broad Ax gives Wilson's side, Dziennik Chicagoski the court's.

versions.value: He refused the bailiff's request and was then seized and beaten
He repeatedly ignored the judge and resisted the bailiff before police joined in

conflicts.note: The resistance claim appears only in the Polish daily's court-side account.

versions.value: Intends to sue the inspector, a sergeant and several patrolmen (15 September)
Has brought suit in the circuit court for $10,000 against Lavin, Cannon, McCann and other officers (19 September)

conflicts.note: The later report likely reflects the suit having been filed in the intervening days.
